title: Tax the bakers. Who pays?
hook: The law says bakers hand over the $2. Do buyers feel any of it?

knows: a market price is where what buyers want meets what sellers make
a per-item tax adds a fixed amount to each sale
doesNotKnow: that who is legally taxed does not decide who bears the tax
that the split depends on how strongly each side reacts to price

misconception: If bakers pay the tax, bakers bear all of it.
objective: The learner can explain that a per-item tax opens a gap between what buyers pay and what sellers keep, that the market splits that gap the same way whichever side hands the money over, and that the side that reacts less to price carries more of it.

claims.text: In the toy market (buyers want 100 − 10p loaves, bakers bake 10p − 20) the price is $6 and 40 loaves sell.
A $2 tax collected from bakers makes buyers pay $7.00 and leaves bakers $5.00; 30 loaves sell.
claims.source: Bakers bake 10(p − 2) − 20 = 10p − 40; 100 − 10p = 10p − 40 gives p = 7; bakers keep 7 − 2 = 5; 100 − 70 = 30. Demo.tsx market("bakers", 10).

claims.text: Collected from buyers instead, the same $2 tax gives the same result: buyers pay $7.00 in total, bakers keep $5.00, 30 loaves sell.
claims.source: Buyers want 100 − 10(p + 2) = 80 − 10p at shelf price p; 80 − 10p = 10p − 20 gives p = 5; buyers pay 5 + 2 = 7. Demo.tsx market("buyers", 10).

claims.text: When buyers react less to price, they carry more of the tax ($1.33 of $2); when they react more, less ($0.67).
claims.source: Demand A − b·p with A = 40 + 6b (keeps the untaxed price at $6), supply 10p − 20. Buyers' share = 2 × 10 / (10 + b): b = 5 gives 1.33, b = 20 gives 0.67. The slopes 5, 10, 20 are illustrative choices.

claims.text: Who bears a tax depends on how strongly each side reacts to price, not on who hands over the money.
claims.source: Tax incidence result for competitive markets with straight-line supply and demand (N. G. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 6 'Supply, Demand, and Government Policies', section on taxes; edition-dependent numbering). Stated as a model result.

claims.text: The lesson is a toy model with straight-line supply and demand and makes no claim about whether any tax is good.
claims.source: Stage chip 'Toy market: straight-line supply and demand'; reveal's last paragraph.

recall.question: A city starts charging coffee shops $0.50 per cup sold. Customers keep buying almost as much coffee whatever it costs. Who ends up carrying most of the $0.50?
options: The shops, because they are the ones who pay the city
The customers, because they barely cut back
recall.why: The tax opens a gap between what customers pay and what shops keep. The side that reacts less to price carries more of it, whoever hands the money over.
